title: Power up: How EU-Africa cooperation can drive Europe’s battery recycling future – European Council on Foreign Relations
gist: Europe's battery-material recycling rates are dismally low despite an EU 2030 target of sourcing 25% of critical raw materials from recycling, leaving it dependent on Chinese-dominated recycling capacity; the author argues Europe must tighten black-mass export rules, urgently build refining capacity, and form recycling partnerships with African countries like Namibia and Kenya to de-risk mineral supply chains faster than mining alone could.

themes.theme: Europe's recycling shortfall vs. policy targets

insights.claim: The European Commission's Critical Raw Materials Act sets a target to source at least 25% of the EU's annual consumption of strategic raw materials from recycling by 2030.
insights.speaker: Sarah Logan
insights.so_what: This is a binding EU policy benchmark investors in battery/mining/recycling supply chains should track for regulatory tailwinds and compliance-driven demand.
insights.quote: it has set an ambitious target to source at least 25% of the EU’s annual consumption of strategic raw materials from recycling by 2030.

insights.claim: A European Court of Auditors report found that seven of 26 energy-transition-related minerals have EU recycling rates of only 1% to 5%, with Europe recovering just three tonnes of natural graphite for every 100 tonnes contained in batteries.
insights.speaker: Sarah Logan
insights.so_what: Extremely low recovery rates signal Europe is far from CRMA targets, implying continued heavy reliance on imported minerals and structural upside for whoever builds EU recycling capacity first.
insights.quote: seven of 26 energy-transition-related minerals have recycling rates between 1% and 5% in the EU
insights.locator: Europe, however, is making little progress

insights.claim: There are ten minerals, including lithium, gallium and silicon metal, that Europe does not recycle at all according to the Court of Auditors report.
insights.speaker: Sarah Logan
insights.so_what: Zero recycling of lithium and other battery-critical minerals is a concrete white-space opportunity for recycling technology and infrastructure investment.
insights.quote: there are another ten minerals that Europe does not recycle at all, including lithium, gallium and silicon metal

insights.claim: Recycling battery materials is much faster to scale than developing new mines elsewhere that produce the same materials, making it a quicker route to reducing dependence on Chinese mineral value chains.
insights.speaker: Sarah Logan
insights.so_what: Recycling capacity investment offers a faster payback timeline for supply-chain de-risking than greenfield mining, favoring recycling-focused capital allocation over long-lead mining projects for near-term diversification.

insights.so_what: Regulatory reclassification of battery materials is a policy catalyst to watch; a shift away from hazardous-waste treatment could unlock investment and lower compliance costs for EU recyclers.

themes.theme: EV feedstock and black-mass export rules

insights.claim: Europe has strong future EV battery feedstock for recycling because it was an early EV adopter: EVs account for 58% of passenger-vehicle sales in Sweden, 56% in Denmark, 48% in the Netherlands, and fully electric vehicles are 22.6% of cars registered across the EU.
insights.speaker: Sarah Logan
insights.so_what: High EV penetration in Nordic/Benelux markets implies a growing domestic pipeline of end-of-life batteries for recyclers, a volume tailwind for EU-based recycling capacity if feedstock is retained domestically.
insights.quote: in Sweden, Denmark and the Netherlands, for example, EVs account for 58%, 56% and 48% of passenger-vehicle sales respectively, while fully electric vehicles comprise 22.6% of cars registered in the EU

insights.claim: In March 2025, the EU reclassified black mass and end-of-life lithium-, nickel- and zinc-based batteries as hazardous waste, prohibiting export of black mass to non-OECD countries and requiring prior notification and consent for shipments within the EU and OECD.
insights.speaker: Sarah Logan
insights.so_what: This 2025 reclassification is a concrete regulatory event that raised export barriers and is a precursor to further restriction proposals discussed later in the article—material for anyone tracking EU critical-minerals policy.
insights.quote: the EU re-classified “black mass”...as “hazardous waste”...This new classification prohibits export of black mass to non-OECD countries

insights.claim: Europe currently exports around 80% of its black mass for refining elsewhere, mostly in Asia, with South Korea a key destination due to its OECD status and cheap recycling capacity.
insights.speaker: Sarah Logan
insights.so_what: The 80% export share of black mass quantifies the scale of value and mineral leakage Europe forgoes, and South Korea's recycling sector is a direct beneficiary of Europe's underinvestment.

insights.claim: The black-mass reclassification has also made it harder to move black mass within Europe, complicating the aggregation of feedstock for domestic recycling even as it restricts exports out of the EU.
insights.speaker: Sarah Logan
insights.so_what: An unintended side effect of the hazardous-waste classification is a logistics bottleneck inside the EU itself, a regulatory friction point that could delay recycling capacity build-out despite good policy intent.

insights.speaker: Sarah Logan
insights.so_what: China's >80% share of global recycling capacity represents a structural chokepoint analogous to its mining/refining dominance—relevant for any thesis on battery supply-chain de-risking away from China.

insights.claim: Hydrometallurgical recycling costs for NMC and LFP batteries are respectively 70% and 67% higher in France than in China, driven by higher labour, energy, environmental compliance, dismantling and transport costs.
insights.speaker: Sarah Logan
insights.so_what: A ~70% cost disadvantage versus China is the core economic barrier that any EU recycling investment thesis must solve for via subsidy, scale, or technology—without it, tighter export rules alone risk stockpiling rather than recycling.
insights.quote: the costs of hydrometallurgical recycling for nickel manganese cobalt (NMC) and lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries are respectively 70% and 67% higher in France than in China

insights.claim: The author argues Europe should implement stricter export restrictions to fully close off black-mass and battery exports and retain products for domestic material recovery, following the US, which in July 2026 empowered federal officials to block exports of end-of-life batteries and e-waste.
insights.speaker: Sarah Logan
insights.so_what: A US precedent (July 2026 export blocking authority) increases the likelihood the EU follows with similar hard export restrictions—watch for EU legislative moves that would further tighten black-mass export policy, benefiting domestic-only recyclers.
insights.quote: The US took this position in July 2026, with President Donald Trump empowering federal officials to block exports of end-of-life batteries and electronic waste to contain these products for recycling within the US.

insights.claim: Europe's hydrometallurgical recycling capacity is less than 3,000 tonnes, around one-sixtieth of China's, while estimates suggest Europe needs 120,000-135,000 tonnes of annual black-mass recycling capacity by 2030.
insights.speaker: Sarah Logan
insights.so_what: This ~40-45x capacity gap versus the 2030 need quantifies a large addressable build-out opportunity for hydrometallurgical recycling infrastructure investment in Europe.

insights.speaker: Sarah Logan
insights.so_what: This is a key risk/caveat for the recycling investment thesis: export restrictions alone are insufficient and must be paired with cost-support mechanisms or the policy could backfire into stranded waste rather than recovered minerals.

insights.speaker: Sarah Logan

themes.theme: Innovation, patents and the European recycler value chain

insights.claim: Patent filings in battery recycling grew 103% in 2026 (adjusted for lag), with China leading applications while US and European companies, notably Belgium's Umicore, are also active.
insights.speaker: Sarah Logan
insights.so_what: A 103% jump in recycling-tech patent filings signals an accelerating innovation race; Umicore stands out as a named European public company positioned in this space alongside Chinese leadership.
insights.quote: 2026 figures showing a 103% growth in filings (adjusted for lag). China leads in patent applications, although US and European companies—notably Belgium’s Umicore—are also active.

insights.claim: European battery recyclers such as Germany's Cylib and Tozero and Norway's Hydrovolt need to establish commercial agreements with EU-based offtakers for recovered minerals, otherwise gains from recycling will be lost if minerals must be exported for lack of domestic buyers.
insights.speaker: Sarah Logan
insights.so_what: Named early-stage European recyclers (Cylib, Tozero, Hydrovolt) are direct plays on this theme, but their success depends on a downstream offtaker value chain that does not yet fully exist—an execution risk for the sector.
insights.quote: European battery recyclers, such as Germany’s Cylib and Tozero and Norway’s Hydrovolt, should identify and establish commercial agreements with EU-based offtakers for the minerals they recover

insights.so_what: A roughly 7.5x growth in stationary storage capacity (to 17x under the SDG7 scenario) implies a rapidly growing future end-of-life battery/e-waste stream in Africa that recycling infrastructure investors should plan capacity around now.

insights.claim: EU-Africa recycling cooperation would benefit African partners by creating jobs, expanding African mineral processing capabilities, and linking African mineral supply chains with European industry, while also helping manage growing e-waste from solar panels, energy-storage batteries and small EVs.
insights.speaker: Sarah Logan
insights.so_what: The mutual-benefit framing (jobs, capability transfer, e-waste management) strengthens the case for durable EU-Africa recycling partnerships as a policy-backed, bilaterally incentivized investment channel rather than a one-sided extraction model.

insights.claim: Successful Africa-Europe recycling partnerships require formalising collection and storage supply chains, building shredding facilities, developing black-mass refining capability, and building workforce skills and local-firm capabilities for the full supply chain.
insights.speaker: Sarah Logan
insights.so_what: This is a checklist of prerequisites (logistics, shredding, refining, workforce) that defines where capital and development-finance support would need to be deployed for EU-Africa recycling partnerships to actually deliver mineral supply, useful for structuring project pipelines.

insights.claim: For Europe, increased mineral recovery both domestically and through African recycling partnerships would deliver supply-chain diversification and faster de-risking from Chinese mineral supply chains than continued reliance on global mine development.
insights.speaker: Sarah Logan
insights.so_what: This is the article's overarching investment thesis: recycling plus African partnerships is framed as the faster, more achievable de-risking path from China versus waiting on new mine supply—an actionable framing for critical-minerals portfolio strategy.
insights.quote: the increased recovery of critical minerals both domestically and through recycling partnerships with African countries offers greater supply chain diversification, access to minerals from non-OECD black mass and de-risking from Chinese mineral supply chains
